qs.q: What are the two main types of hydatidiform mole classified under gestational trophoblastic disease?
o: Ascending and haematogenous
Complete and partial types
Endometrioid and Brenner
Serous and mucinous types
qs.e: Hydatidiform moles are divided into complete and partial types. Serous and mucinous refer to types of ovarian surface epithelial tumors.
qs.s: Outline of Female Reproductive Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A pathology resident reviews a complete hydatidiform mole specimen. Which cytogenetic and morphological feature is characteristic of a complete mole?
o: Triploid karyotype with identifiable fetal parts
46,XY maternal origin with early embryonic remnants
46,XX paternal origin with no fetal parts
Diploid karyotype showing prominent fetal red blood cells
qs.e: A complete hydatidiform mole has a 46,XX karyotype derived entirely from paternal genetic material and lacks fetal parts. Partial moles are typically triploid and contain fetal parts.
qs.s: Medical Pathology Final Revision: Chemical, Hema, Systemic: MCQs

qs.q: A pathology specimen from a clinical case shows a complete molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole). What is the underlying genetic basis for this condition?
o: Maternal chromosomes outnumbering paternal
Trisomy of an autosome by error
Complete deletion of sex chromosomes
Paternal chromosomes predominating over maternal
qs.e: A hydatidiform mole occurs when the paternal set of chromosomes outnumbers or predominates over the maternal set. It is not caused by a simple autosomal trisomy or maternal chromosome excess.
qs.s: PAT III — Progress Assessment Test (8 November 2019) — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A pathology laboratory is analyzing a complete hydatidiform mole (molar pregnancy). What is the underlying genetic basis for a complete mole?
o: Monosomy X resulting from complete loss of the maternal sex chromosome
Entirely paternal set of chromosomes (androgenetic) making it diploid
Tetraploid cell division error during early embryonic cleavage stages
Triploid composition resulting from fertilization by two sperm cells
qs.e: A complete hydatidiform mole is entirely paternal (androgenetic) and diploid, where the paternal set of chromosomes predominates over the maternal set. A partial mole is typically triploid from dispermy.
qs.s: PAT III — Progress Assessment Test (8 November 2019) — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A complete hydatidiform mole differs from a partial mole in that a complete mole
o: Is triploid and contains some normal chorionic villi
Results from a normal egg fertilised by two spermatozoa
Contains foetal parts and has scalloped villous margins
Is diploid with all genetic content of paternal origin
qs.e: A complete mole is diploid (46,XX or 46,XY) with all chromosomes of paternal origin, arising when two spermatozoa or a diploid sperm fertilise an empty egg.

qs.q: What percentage of complete hydatidiform moles progress to give rise to choriocarcinoma?
o: Between 20 and 30%
Around 10 to 15%
Approximately 2 to 3%
Less than 1%
qs.e: 80–90% of moles resolve after curettage. 10% of complete moles are invasive, but only 2–3% give rise to choriocarcinoma.

qs.q: Gestational choriocarcinoma differs histologically from hydatidiform mole because choriocarcinoma
o: Shows hydropic swelling of chorionic villi
Demonstrates scalloped villous margins with focal atypia
Has focal trophoblastic proliferation around normal villi
Contains no chorionic villi and is composed of anaplastic trophoblasts
qs.e: Choriocarcinoma contains no chorionic villi. It is composed entirely of anaplastic cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts invading the myometrium and vessels.

es.q: What are the two main types of hydatidiform mole? → Complete and Partial.
es.m:
- **Complete Mole**: Results from fertilization of an empty oocyte by a single sperm that duplicates, or two sperm, containing only paternal chromosomes (4XX or 4XY).
- **Morphology**: Characterized by diffusely swollen, hydropic chorionic villi and a complete absence of fetal parts.
- **Malignant Potential**: Carries a significantly higher risk of developing into gestational choriocarcinoma.
- **Partial Mole**: Results from fertilization of a normal oocyte by two sperm, usually resulting in a triploid karyotype (69,XXY).
- **Morphology**: Shows a mixture of normal and hydropic villi, often accompanied by identifiable fetal tissue or parts, with a lower risk of malignancy.
